question.prompt:
In \(\triangle ABC,\) \(AB=6,\) \(BC=7,\) and \(CA=8.\) Point \(D\) lies on \(\overline{BC},\) and \(\overline{AD}\) bisects \(\angle BAC.\) Point \(E\) lies on \(\overline{AC},\) and \(\overline{BE}\) bisects \(\angle ABC.\) The bisectors intersect at \(F.\) What is the ratio \(AF:FD?\)

[Figure 1](figures/2016_AMC_12A_Q12_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
The useful observation is that \(BF\) also bisects the angle at \(B\) in the smaller triangle \(ABD\), because \(D\) lies on \(BC\).

[Figure 1](figures/2016_AMC_12A_Q12_question_fig1.svg)

The angle bisector theorem says that an internal angle bisector divides the opposite side in the ratio of the adjacent sides. Applying it to \(AD\) in \(\triangle ABC\) gives
\[
BD:DC=AB:AC=6:8=3:4.
\]
Since \(BD+DC=BC=7\), the seven ratio parts each have length \(1\). Thus \(BD=3\) and \(DC=4\).

Now \(\angle ABD=\angle ABC\), and \(BF\) lies along the given bisector \(BE\). Therefore \(BF\) is the internal angle bisector in \(\triangle ABD\), meeting its opposite side \(AD\) at \(F\). Applying the theorem again gives
\[
AF:FD=AB:BD=6:3=\boxed{2:1}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
solutions.title: Apply the angle bisector theorem twice
